# How to rehearse a hard conversation with ChatGPT

> **In short:** You can rehearse a tough talk — a raise, an apology, a breakup — out loud with ChatGPT's voice mode, then ask for feedback on your tone. Free users get limited voice time; longer sessions are on paid plans.

There's a moment before every hard conversation when your heart beats faster and your mouth goes dry. With ChatGPT's voice mode, you can practice the actual words out loud, hear how they sound, and ask for feedback before the real talk happens. It's not therapy, and it won't deliver the message for you — but a few minutes of honest rehearsal can change how the whole conversation feels.

## Before you start
- A ChatGPT account — the free plan works for a short practice, paid plans give you more voice time.
- The ChatGPT mobile app on your phone (voice mode is most reliable there), or a browser at chatgpt.com.
- A quiet spot where you can speak out loud without feeling self-conscious.
- About 10–15 minutes, plus the conversation you're building toward.

## Step 1 — Open ChatGPT and start a fresh chat
Open the ChatGPT app on your phone, or go to chatgpt.com in a browser. Tap "New chat" — it usually lives at the top of the screen, often as a pencil icon or a "+" button. A blank message box appears, ready for your first message. Starting fresh matters because the assistant will use everything you write in this chat to shape its replies, so an old conversation can lead it in confusing directions. If you don't see a "New chat" button, the app may have opened straight into one — that's fine, just start typing.
💬 Example: don't write anything yet — just confirm the screen is empty and the cursor is blinking.
You'll know it worked when you see an empty message box with a blinking cursor and no prior messages above it.

## Step 2 — Tell ChatGPT the situation and who you're talking to
Type a short scene-setter: who the other person is, what the conversation is about, and the outcome you want. The more concrete you are, the better its feedback later. After you hit send, ChatGPT usually replies with a couple of clarifying questions or a first draft of what you could say. Read its reply before moving on — it will quietly check that it understood the situation. If the reply shows it has the wrong idea (it thought you wanted career advice when you actually wanted to apologize to your sister), correct it before you start rehearsing.
💬 Example: "I need to ask my manager for a raise. I've been at the company three years, took on the whole client-onboarding process, and a recruiter just offered me more money elsewhere. Help me rehearse this conversation out loud and give me tips on sounding calm."
You'll know it worked when ChatGPT confirms the setup and asks a useful follow-up question, or jumps straight into a draft opening line.

## Step 3 — Turn on voice mode
Now switch from typing to talking. In the ChatGPT mobile app, look for a sound-wave or microphone icon near the message box and tap it once. A round "Listening…" indicator appears, and the keyboard slides out of the way. On the web version, voice mode may sit inside a headphones icon next to the message field. Voice isn't just a nicety — saying the words out loud is the whole point, because that's exactly what you'll do in the real conversation. If voice mode is greyed out, your free daily minutes may be used up; you can still keep typing and the practice still works, just less powerfully.
💬 Example: tap the sound-wave icon, wait for the listening ring, then say "Hi, are you ready to start the rehearsal?"
You'll know it worked when ChatGPT greets you out loud and your spoken words appear as text on the screen at the same time.

## Step 4 — Practice saying the words out loud
Take a breath and say the opening line you actually plan to use. Don't aim for perfect — the goal is to hear yourself say it. ChatGPT will respond in the role you set up in Step 2, and you can keep going back and forth like a real conversation. If you freeze, just say "I'm stuck, give me a calmer opening sentence." Keep practicing until the words start to feel like yours rather than a script you memorized. If voice mode cuts out mid-sentence, tap the icon again to resume — it picks up roughly where you left off.
💬 Example: say "I wanted to talk to you about my salary. Over the past year I took on the whole onboarding flow, and I'd like to talk about adjusting my pay to reflect that."
You'll know it worked when you've said the hard part at least once out loud without your voice shaking or trailing off.

## Step 5 — Ask for feedback on how it sounded
After one full run-through, ask ChatGPT to step out of role and give you feedback. Be specific: ask about tone, pacing, and word choice. The assistant can flag phrases that sound aggressive, apologetic, or unclear, and suggest softer alternatives. It can also point out if you rambled, repeated yourself, or skipped the main point. Listen to the feedback with the same attention you gave the rehearsal — this is where most of the learning happens. If a suggestion feels wrong (it may propose lines that don't sound like you at all), just say "that isn't me — give me two other options that are simpler."
💬 Example: "Step out of the role-play now. Tell me three things I did well, two things to soften, and one phrase I should swap out for something calmer."
You'll know it worked when you get a short, specific list — usually two or three concrete changes you can actually make.

## Step 6 — Write down your final version
Take the best lines from the practice, plus any improvements from the feedback, and write them into a short note on your phone. Don't draft a long script — short bullets you'll glance at before the real talk work far better. Keep the note where you'll see it the morning of the conversation: your Notes app, a pinned message to yourself, or the top of your reminders. ChatGPT can't send the message for you, can't be in the room during the real conversation, and can't predict exactly how the other person will react — what it can do is help you rehearse until the words feel natural and you trust yourself to deliver them.
💬 Example: three short bullets — "1. Thank them for the time. 2. State the ask: a raise that matches my current scope. 3. Pause and let them respond before explaining the recruiter offer."
You'll know it worked when you have a small, scannable note that feels like something you would actually say, not a corporate template.

## Common mistakes
- Skipping voice mode and only typing the script. Typed drafts feel fine on screen, but they often crumble the moment you say them out loud. Always do at least one spoken run, even if it feels awkward.
- Asking for the "perfect" script. There isn't one. The goal is to find words that sound like you, not a polished template you'll stumble over. If a line doesn't feel natural, throw it out.
- Only rehearsing the easy part. Most hard conversations fall apart when the other person pushes back. Ask ChatGPT to play someone who says no, and rehearse your response to that — that's usually the moment that decides the whole talk.

## What this means for you
- **In everyday life:** any conversation that's been sitting in your head for days — a late bill, a noisy neighbor, a relative who overstepped — can be practiced in five minutes before you actually have it. The dread drops sharply once you've said the words once.
- **For your business or work:** salary talks, project pushback, and feedback conversations all benefit from one rehearsal. People who have practiced out loud even once sound noticeably calmer and more direct, and the other person picks up on that immediately.
- **If you're just getting started:** pick the smallest hard conversation on your list — a refund request, a missed deadline you need to explain. Five minutes of practice beats five days of dread, and the second one is always faster than the first.

## Try it now
Open ChatGPT, start a new chat, and paste this: "Help me rehearse a two-minute conversation where I tell my friend I can't lend them money again. After each attempt, give me short feedback on tone. Start now and play the role of my friend." Then try it once out loud — even if it's only 30 seconds.
